name: Keith Thomas
specialization: English magical beliefs; witchcraft in context of religious change and popular culture

major_works.title: Religion and the Decline of Magic
major_works.significance: Foundational 800-page survey placing English witchcraft and magic within the full context of popular religious belief and the Reformation

major_works.title: Man and the Natural World: Changing Attitudes in England 1500-1800
major_works.significance: Extends social history methodology to attitudes toward nature

core_argument: English witchcraft accusations arose from the social tensions created by the decline of Catholic magical services after the Reformation, combined with the 'charity refused' mechanism: when a householder refused charity to a poor neighbor who then suffered misfortune, guilt was projected onto the refused beggar as a witch. Witchcraft filled the gap left by the Church's lost magical remedies.

methodological_approach.primary_materials: Parish records, court records, pamphlet literature, ecclesiastical depositions across England 1500-1700
methodological_approach.analysis_target: Social function of magical belief; relationship between religious change and witchcraft; charity and community obligation
methodological_approach.evidence_type: Wide-ranging qualitative survey of print and archival sources; contextual social analysis
methodological_approach.explanatory_level: Sociological-functional: beliefs serve social needs created by structural changes

key_contributions.claim: The typical English witch accusation followed a pattern: a householder refused charity to a poor woman, she cursed or muttered on leaving, the householder later suffered misfortune, guilt about the refusal was converted into accusation
key_contributions.implication: Witchcraft accusations reflect guilt and psychological projection by accusers, not evidence of witches' malice

key_contributions.claim: The Reformation removed Catholic magical services (blessings, holy water, saints' intercession) that had managed anxiety about illness and misfortune; witchcraft belief and cunning folk filled this vacuum
key_contributions.implication: English witchcraft must be understood in the context of religious change, not in isolation

key_contributions.claim: Pre-modern magical beliefs were rational responses to real problems of illness, crop failure, and uncertainty in the absence of alternative explanations
key_contributions.implication: Magic should be analyzed functionally and sympathetically, not dismissed as superstition

reception_and_critique.major_influences: Social anthropology (Evans-Pritchard), sociology of religion (Weber), Annales social history
criticisms: Charity-refused thesis critiqued as overly schematic; not all cases fit the pattern
English focus limits applicability to Continental patterns
Later scholars (Clark) argued Thomas underweights the theological sophistication of demonological thought
Feminist historians argued insufficient attention to gender dynamics

historiographical_significance: Thomas's Religion and the Decline of Magic remains one of the most cited works in early modern English history and established social history methodology for studying magical belief. Its scope, ambition, and empirical depth set a standard that subsequent regional studies aimed to match or refine. The charity-refused thesis influenced Macfarlane and remains a reference point in community-level analyses.
source_method: Published scholarship and critical historiographical reconstruction
